title: Freeing the captives, 1761
hookLine: after Panipat, Sikh horsemen freed women being taken away by Abdali's army and returned them home

lines: PANIPAT, AND AN ARMY HEADING HOME.
cards: Here's a question that sounds easy until it's real. You've just pulled someone out of danger. They're frightened, far from home, and for the moment completely in your hands.
What happens next? Tradition says Sikh riders faced exactly that after a great battle at Panipat, which Abdali's army had won.
Heading home to Afghanistan, the army took captive women with it, and Sikh horsemen struck and set them free. The raid is the well-known part. The tradition dwells on what came after it.

teach.h: THEY HAD NO STAKE IN PANIPAT.
teach.b: Last week, Sikh riders struck a departing Persian army and walked its captives home. This story asks a harder question: what kind of men were the rescuers, once the rescue was done?

teach.h: FREED AS THE ARMY CROSSED THE RIVERS.
teach.b: Tradition says Sikh horsemen fell on the rear of Abdali's army as it crossed the rivers of Punjab, and freed the women it was taking away. The Sikhs had no stake in that battle at Panipat.
These weren't their wives or their sisters. They rode anyway. Then came the real test.

Once free, the women were in the hands of armed men in a lawless time, far from home. Anything could have happened. Tradition says the Sikhs gave them food and escort, and took them back to their own families.
Not kept. Not claimed. Brought home.
Why does the tradition make so much of that? Because Sikh tradition measures the Khalsa by how it treats the defenseless.
Bhai Gurdas, describing the true Sikh in his Vars, says, in paraphrase, that when he sees other people's women, he looks on them as mothers, sisters and daughters.
That was the standard. For the women in the story, it meant something very concrete: a door opening in their own village, and their own people standing in it. Notice the order of the story.
The freeing was quick. The bringing home took long walking, care and restraint. Freedom is the start.
Brought home safe is the finish.

how: Sikhs tell the story of the freed captives in gurdwara talks as an example of the Khalsa's duty to protect the defenseless, alongside the teaching that a Sikh regards other women as mothers, sisters and daughters.

o: a soldier who guards the rear of a marching army
a gift of food given to travelers on the road
a captive, someone taken and held against their will

games.q: freed, then brought home — tap the pairs.

s: the Sikhs rode out because the captives were their own families
the Sikhs had no stake in Panipat. they rode anyway.
Bhai Gurdas says a Sikh looks on other people's women as mothers, sisters and daughters
that was the standard the tradition holds the riders to.
the freeing was the whole of the story
tradition dwells on what came after: care and restraint until they were home.

games.q: you're a Sikh rider. you've freed a line of captive women as an army crossed the rivers, far from their homes. what now?
o: feed them, guard them, and take them back to their families.
leave them at the nearest town and go.
games.why: tradition says the Sikhs escorted them home to their own families, and the story is remembered for that restraint as much as for the raid.

practice: Bring to mind someone being pushed around a little, at work, at school, online, in your own family, talked over, underpaid, mocked or used; they don't have to be yours to defend, and that's the point.

Picture one thing you could do, a word in a meeting, a message, a refusal to laugh along, and then the second half: staying with them afterward, until they're steady. If you pray, hold them in mind and say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: bandi, a captive. Tradition says Sikh horsemen freed women being carried off by Abdali's army, then fed them, guarded them, and returned them to their families. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bandi, a captive or prisoner; the same word is in Bandi Chhor, the release of prisoners.

carryVoice: Your line: brought home safe. Restraint is part of the rescue. Day eight hundred sixty-four, done.

sources.ref: The freeing of captives after Panipat, Sikh tradition
